subject: Science
period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 45 minutes × 14 periods = 630 minutes
Total: 14 periods · 10h 30min

periods.activity_title: The Box Experiment — Discovering Push and Pull
periods.activity_description: Students attempt to move a large cardboard box in as many ways as possible, recording each mode of movement. They discover that every action — pushing, pulling, lifting, carrying — involves either a push or a pull, and articulate a first definition of force.

roles.role_description: Sets up the cardboard box, prompts students to try different modes of movement, and guides the class discussion toward naming each action as a push or pull.
In small groups, attempt different ways to move the box, record their observations, and share what they noticed about the actions involved.

time_bands.activity: Teacher introduces the box and invites groups to try moving it in as many ways as they can think of.
Groups attempt pushing, pulling, lifting, and carrying the box, recording each mode of movement and the action required.
Class discussion: each group shares one mode; teacher maps all modes onto 'push' or 'pull' on the board.
Students individually write a one-sentence definition of force using the class observations as evidence.

periods.teacher_notes: This opening unit anchors the chapter in direct physical experience — every student should try at least one mode of moving the box before the discussion. Watch for students who conflate 'lift' as a separate type of force rather than seeing it as an upward push; redirect by asking what their hand is doing to the box. Groups ready to move on can be asked to name which body part applies the force in each case.

periods.activity_title: What Does a Force Actually Do? — Analysing Everyday Situations
periods.activity_description: Students examine a structured set of everyday force situations — a friend stopping a bicycle, hitting a ball with a bat, pressing an inflated balloon — and record what changes each force produces. They categorise the observed effects into four types: initiating motion, changing speed, changing direction, and changing shape.

roles.role_description: Presents each scenario in sequence, poses the guiding question 'what changed when the force was applied?', and consolidates the four effect categories on the board.
Examines each scenario, records the observed effect in their own words, and attempts to group effects into categories before the class consolidation.

time_bands.activity: Brief recall of the previous unit's definition; teacher introduces the guiding question for this unit.
Students work individually through the three force scenarios, recording what changed in each case.
Pairs compare their categorisations and negotiate a shared list of distinct effect types.
Class consolidation — teacher builds the four effect categories from student responses and students copy the finalised list.

periods.teacher_notes: This unit builds directly on the previous unit's definition: now students ask not just what force is, but what it does. A common error is listing 'stopping an object' and 'slowing it down' as different effects; guide students to see both as changes in speed. The checkpoint is whether each student can map all three scenarios onto the four-effect framework before the unit closes.

periods.stage_label: Classify forces by contact and non-contact
periods.activity_title: How Many Objects? — Force as Interaction
periods.activity_description: Students revisit each force situation from the previous unit and count the objects involved, inferring that at least two objects must interact for a force to occur. They refine the definition of force as arising from interaction, learn the SI unit (newton, N), and encounter the idea that both objects in an interaction experience forces that vanish when interaction ends.

roles.role_description: Guides students through the object-counting exercise, introduces the formal definition of force as interaction, and presents the newton as the SI unit.
Re-examines the previous unit's force scenarios, counts the objects involved in each, and records how the revised definition extends their earlier understanding.

time_bands.activity: Students open their notebooks to the previous unit's scenarios and count the number of objects involved in each force situation.
Class discussion of counts — teacher draws out the pattern that every force involves at least two objects.
Teacher introduces the formal definition (force as interaction), the SI unit newton, and the Step Further point about mutual forces disappearing when interaction ends.
Students revise their earlier one-sentence definition to incorporate the interaction idea and the SI unit, then share with a neighbour.

periods.teacher_notes: This unit bridges the observational work of the first two units to the formal concept: force is not a property of one object but a product of interaction. Students often think only one object in a pair 'has' the force; prompt them to identify what the second object does to the first. The revised definition students write here will serve as their working reference throughout the classification stage ahead.

periods.stage_label: Classify forces by contact and non-contact
periods.activity_title: Muscles at Work — Investigating Muscular Force
periods.activity_description: Students perform a series of physical actions — walking, lifting, pushing, gripping — and identify which muscles contract or elongate in each, establishing muscular force as a contact force requiring physical contact. They extend the category to animal muscular force and internal body functions, sorting examples onto a class chart.

roles.role_description: Leads the class through the action sequence, names the muscular force category, and facilitates sorting of human, animal, and internal examples.
Perform each physical action, feel and describe the muscular effort involved, and contribute examples to the class sorting chart.

time_bands.activity: Students perform a sequence of actions (lift a book, push a desk, grip a pen tightly) and describe the sensation in their muscles.
Teacher introduces 'muscular force' as the first contact force; groups brainstorm and list examples involving animals, birds, fish, and internal body functions.
Groups contribute examples to a shared class sorting chart under categories: human movement, animal movement, internal body functions.
Students write a definition of muscular force in their own words and give one example not mentioned in class.

periods.teacher_notes: The previous unit established that forces require interaction between two objects; this unit now names the first specific force type that arises from physical contact. Watch for students who overlook internal muscular forces (heartbeat, digestion) as genuine forces — ask them what the heart is doing to blood to push it through the body. A useful checkpoint: can students state what two objects are interacting in each muscular force example?
materials: Books or small objects for lifting

periods.stage_label: Classify forces by contact and non-contact
periods.activity_description: Students push an object across several different surfaces (glass, cloth, wood, ceramic tile, sand) and observe how the stopping distance varies with the surface. They record the pattern, identify friction as the contact force opposing motion, and examine why friction exists by linking it to surface irregularities.

roles.role_description: Sets up the surface comparison activity, introduces friction as the force responsible for stopping, and explains the mechanism of interlocking surface irregularities.
Push an object across each surface with a consistent effort, measure or compare stopping distances, and record which surface produces the most and least friction.

time_bands.activity: Teacher poses the question: why do moving objects stop on their own even when no one is touching them? Students suggest ideas.
Groups push an object across each prepared surface in turn, record the stopping distance, and rank surfaces from least to most friction.
Class shares rankings; teacher introduces friction as a contact force that always opposes motion and explains the surface-irregularity mechanism.
Students write a causal explanation: 'Object X stopped fastest on surface Y because…' incorporating the irregularity mechanism.

periods.teacher_notes: This unit is a direct extension of the muscular force unit — both are contact forces, but friction differs in that students did not apply it consciously. The key misconception to address is that smoother surfaces have no friction; the chapter explains that even smooth surfaces have minute irregularities. Groups that finish ranking quickly can be asked to predict what would happen on a surface covered in oil or wet soap and justify their prediction.
materials: Samples of glass, cloth, wood, ceramic tile, sand on flat boards

periods.stage_label: Classify forces by contact and non-contact
periods.activity_title: Forces Without Touching — Magnetic and Electrostatic Force
periods.activity_description: Students stack ring magnets on a vertical stick with like poles facing and observe the upper magnet floating, then rub a plastic scale with polythene and observe it attracting paper pieces without contact. They compare the two phenomena and classify both as non-contact forces, identifying the conditions (charges or magnetic poles) under which attraction or repulsion occurs.

roles.role_description: Sets up the ring-magnet stack and the charged-scale demonstration, then guides students to extract the shared characteristic that neither requires physical contact.
Observe both demonstrations, record what is attracted or repelled and under what conditions, and attempt to classify each as contact or non-contact before the teacher confirms.

time_bands.activity: Groups observe the floating ring magnet and record what they see; teacher prompts: 'Is there any contact between the upper magnet and anything pushing it up?'
Students rub a plastic scale with polythene, bring it near paper pieces without touching, and observe attraction; they then rub two balloons with woollen cloth and observe repulsion.
Groups compare both phenomena and write a shared statement about what magnetic force and electrostatic force have in common.
Class discussion consolidates the non-contact category; teacher provides formal definitions of magnetic force and electrostatic force.

periods.teacher_notes: Students come to this unit knowing magnets from Grade 6, so the floating-magnet demonstration is a productive surprise that extends familiar knowledge. A frequent confusion is treating magnetic force and electrostatic force as the same thing simply because both are non-contact; ask groups to name one condition under which each operates that does not apply to the other. Students ready to move on should be able to give a counter-example — an object magnetic force cannot attract that electrostatic force can.
materials: Two ring magnets and a vertical stick

periods.stage_label: Classify forces by contact and non-contact
periods.activity_description: Students throw a ball upward several times and observe its complete trajectory — rising, pausing, then accelerating back down — regardless of throwing force. They infer that an unseen force continuously acts downward, identify it as gravitational force, and contrast it with magnetic and electrostatic force by noting that gravity is always attractive and never repulsive.

roles.role_description: Frames the inquiry question about why the ball always returns, guides students through the trajectory observations, and formalises the definition of gravitational force.

Throws the ball and carefully observes each phase of its motion, records the direction of the force inferred at each phase, and writes a comparison of gravity with the other non-contact forces studied.

time_bands.activity: Each student throws a ball upward and observes its trajectory; teacher asks them to describe the motion at three points: going up, at the top, coming down.
Students record at each phase what force must be acting (direction and effect) and whether that force is contact or non-contact.
Class discussion builds the definition of gravitational force; teacher highlights the vertical-motion description (slows, stops, reverses, accelerates downward).
Students write a comparison: 'Gravitational force is similar to / different from magnetic and electrostatic force because…' with at least two points of contrast.

periods.teacher_notes: This unit closes the non-contact forces strand and rounds out the full classification stage; students should now hold all five force types in their minds as a coherent system. The critical misconception here is that the force on the ball disappears at the top of its trajectory — students often think the ball 'has no force' at its highest point; press them to explain why it then falls rather than staying up. The contrast writing task checks whether students are comparing properties (always attractive, never repulsive) rather than just restating definitions.
materials: A rubber ball or tennis ball
homework: Using the five-force classification from this unit, identify two forces acting during the act of swimming and write one sentence explaining whether each is contact or non-contact and what two objects are interacting.

periods.stage_label: Measure weight and distinguish mass from weight
periods.activity_title: Spring Stretch — Sensing Gravitational Pull on Different Objects
periods.activity_description: Students hang different objects (pencil box, tiffin box, small stone) from a spring in sequence and observe that each stretches the spring by a different amount. They record the pattern and infer that Earth pulls different objects with different forces, establishing weight as the force of Earth's gravitational pull on an object measured in newtons.

roles.role_description: Sets up the spring and guides students to connect the varying stretch to the varying gravitational pull, introducing weight as a measurable force.
Hang each object in turn, observe and record the stretch, rank objects by the gravitational pull they experience, and propose what quantity the stretch is measuring.

time_bands.activity: Teacher poses the question: do all objects experience the same gravitational pull? Students predict and record their prediction.
Groups hang each object from the spring in turn, observe the stretch, and record relative rankings.
Class compares rankings and the teacher formalises weight as the gravitational force on an object, measured in newtons.
Students write a sentence explaining what the spring stretch represents in force terms and why different objects produce different stretches.

periods.teacher_notes: This unit opens the measurement strand; students bring the gravitational force concept from the previous stage and now ask how to quantify it. A common confusion is treating a bigger stretch as meaning the spring is 'stronger'; redirect by asking what the spring is responding to — the Earth's pull on the object, not a property of the spring itself. Groups that correctly rank objects can be asked to predict whether the spring stretch would be the same on the Moon, prompting the upcoming mass-versus-weight distinction.

periods.stage_label: Measure weight and distinguish mass from weight
periods.activity_title: Reading the Spring Balance — Range, Least Count, and Measurement
periods.activity_description: Students examine a spring balance, identify its range and calculate its least count, then measure the weight of several objects and record readings in newtons. They practise correct reading technique, compare their readings, and convert their qualitative rankings from the previous unit into numerical weight values.

roles.role_description: Introduces the spring balance's parts (hook, spring, graduated scale), demonstrates correct reading technique, and guides the range and least-count identification.
Examine the spring balance, identify range and least count, measure the weight of each provided object, and record readings in a table.

time_bands.activity: Teacher describes the spring balance's structure and demonstrates how to read the scale correctly, including what 'range' and 'least count' mean.
Groups identify the range and calculate the least count of their spring balance, then measure the weight of each object and record in a table (object, reading in N).
Groups compare their weight readings and check whether the numerical ranking matches their qualitative spring-stretch ranking from the previous unit.
Students write a short procedure: how to find the least count of a spring balance and why it matters when recording a measurement.

periods.teacher_notes: This unit follows directly from the spring-stretch observation: students now replace qualitative comparison with a calibrated instrument. Watch for students reading the scale from an angle and getting parallax errors — emphasise eye-level reading. The checkpoint is whether each student can calculate least count independently before measuring; groups that cannot should be supported before they record readings.

periods.stage_label: Measure weight and distinguish mass from weight
periods.activity_title: Mass Is Not Weight — Distinguishing Two Different Quantities
periods.activity_description: Students examine the claim that the same 1 kg object weighs 10 N on Earth, 1.6 N on the Moon, and 25.4 N on Jupiter, and construct a principled distinction between mass (amount of matter, constant everywhere, measured in kg) and weight (gravitational force, varies by location, measured in N). They apply the distinction to classify given statements as referring to mass or weight.

roles.role_description: Presents the planet weight data, explains the conceptual distinction between mass and weight, and works through classification examples with the class.
Studies the planet weight data, articulates the distinction in their own words, and classifies a set of given statements as referring to mass or weight.

time_bands.activity: Teacher presents the planet weight table (Earth 10 N, Moon 1.6 N, Mars 3.8 N, Venus 9 N, Jupiter 25.4 N for a 1 kg object) and asks: what stays the same and what changes?
Teacher explains mass as amount of matter (constant, kg) and weight as gravitational force (varies, N); students take structured notes comparing the two.

Students individually classify a set of statements (e.g. 'The astronaut's body contains the same amount of matter on the Moon as on Earth' vs. 'The astronaut feels lighter on the Moon') as referring to mass or weight, with justification.
Class review of classifications; teacher addresses the most common misclassifications by returning to the defining properties.

periods.teacher_notes: Students arrive at this unit having measured weight with a spring balance; now they must see that what they measured is not the same as what a balance scale measures. The enduring misconception — that mass and weight are the same thing — is directly challenged by the planet data; ask students what a spring balance would read on Jupiter and whether the object's 'amount of matter' has changed. A useful probe: 'Would your mass change if you went to the Moon? Would your weight?'
materials: Planet weight data table (written on board or printed)
homework: A 5 kg bag of rice is weighed on Earth and then taken to the Moon. Write two sentences: one stating what would change and one stating what would not change, giving the reason for each.

periods.stage_label: Explain floating and sinking through competing forces
periods.activity_title: The Bottle in the Bucket — Feeling Upthrust
periods.activity_description: Students push a sealed empty bottle into a bucket of water, feel the upward push, release the bottle, and observe it bounce back to the surface. They identify the upward force as upthrust or buoyant force and compare its direction to the direction of gravitational force acting on the same object.

roles.role_description: Sets up the bucket activity, introduces 'upthrust' and 'buoyant force' as the formal names for the felt upward push, and connects the observation to the gravitational force acting downward.
Take turns pushing the bottle down, describe the force felt, release the bottle, and record both the upward and downward forces acting on the bottle at the moment of release.

time_bands.activity: Teacher presents the bottle and bucket; groups predict what will happen when the bottle is pushed under water and then released.

Each student in the group pushes the bottle under water, describes the force felt, and observes the bottle's behaviour on release; groups record both the direction of the force they felt and the direction of the bottle's movement.
Class shares observations; teacher introduces upthrust and buoyant force, drawing a simple force diagram showing gravity downward and buoyant force upward.
Students annotate a diagram of the bottle in water, labelling gravitational force (direction, cause) and buoyant force (direction, cause).

periods.teacher_notes: This unit opens the final stage and introduces a new force type that students feel directly — a strong experiential anchor. Connect explicitly to the classification stage: buoyant force is a contact force, the liquid and the bottle are the two interacting objects. Watch for students who think the bottle floats because it is 'light' rather than because buoyant force exceeds gravitational force; the force-diagram annotation is the checkpoint for this.

periods.stage_label: Explain floating and sinking through competing forces
periods.activity_title: Sink or Float? — Reasoning About Competing Forces
periods.activity_description: Students are given a set of objects of varying materials and sizes and predict whether each will sink or float, then test their predictions. They explain each outcome by comparing the gravitational force and buoyant force acting on the object, and investigate how the density of the liquid affects the buoyant force.

roles.role_description: Provides the set of objects and guides students to move from observational prediction to force-based explanation, introducing density as a determinant of buoyant force.
Predict, test, and record outcomes for each object, then construct a force-comparison explanation for each prediction that proved correct and each that was wrong.

time_bands.activity: Each group predicts sink or float for each object and records a one-phrase reason based on their current understanding.
Groups test each object in water, record whether prediction matched outcome, and write a force-comparison explanation for each using 'gravitational force' and 'buoyant force'.
Teacher introduces the role of liquid density in determining buoyant force; groups discuss how their explanations would change in a denser liquid such as salt water.
Students revise any incorrect pre-test explanations using the force-comparison framework, then share one revision with the class.

periods.teacher_notes: The previous unit gave students the names and directions of the two competing forces; this unit asks them to use those forces to reason about outcomes. The most productive misconceptions are size-based ('big things sink') and material-based ('metal always sinks') — both can be challenged by including a large cork and a small metal ball in the test set. The checkpoint is the quality of the revision: does the student's corrected explanation name both forces and state which is greater?
materials: Various objects: cork, small metal ball, wooden block, plastic bottle cap, clay ball, pumice if available

periods.stage_label: Explain floating and sinking through competing forces
periods.activity_title: Archimedes' Principle — The Displaced Liquid Rule
periods.activity_description: Students examine Archimedes' Principle — the upward force on an immersed object equals the weight of the liquid it displaces — and use it to predict outcomes for objects of different densities. They explain why pumice floats despite being rock, connecting the air-pocket density argument to the force-balance framework.

roles.role_description: States and explains Archimedes' Principle, works through the pumice example, and connects the principle to the density comparison framework established in the previous unit.
Takes structured notes, applies the principle to a set of prediction tasks, and writes a causal explanation for the pumice floating phenomenon.

time_bands.activity: Teacher presents Archimedes' Principle — upward force equals weight of displaced liquid — and illustrates it by connecting to the bottle experiment: when the bottle displaces more water than its own weight, it floats.
Students apply the principle to a set of prediction tasks: given the weight of an object and the weight of liquid it displaces, predict whether it sinks or floats and explain why.
Teacher presents the pumice example — volcanic rock, air pockets, density less than water — and students write a causal explanation connecting density, displaced weight, and buoyant force.
Pairs share their pumice explanations and identify one element they would add or change after hearing their partner's version.

periods.teacher_notes: This unit elevates the force-balance reasoning of the previous unit to a principled rule that applies generally. Students sometimes confuse 'weight of displaced liquid' with 'weight of the object' — emphasise that the upward force depends on the liquid pushed aside, not on the object's own weight. The pumice explanation is a good check: a strong explanation will name both density and the displaced-weight comparison, not just say 'pumice is light'.

periods.stage_label: Explain floating and sinking through competing forces
periods.activity_title: Forces in Play — Classifying, Measuring, and Explaining Across the Chapter
periods.activity_description: Students work through a rich scenario set in which each situation involves an unknown or unfamiliar force configuration. For each scenario they identify the forces acting, classify them by type, determine which is greater, and predict the outcome — integrating the classification system, the weight-measurement understanding, and the buoyancy framework into a single analytical act.

roles.role_description: Presents the scenario set, circulates to probe reasoning, and facilitates a final class discussion that draws connections across all force types studied.
Works through each scenario independently, writing a structured analysis that names forces, classifies them, compares their magnitudes, and states the predicted outcome with justification.

time_bands.activity: Teacher presents the scenario set and explains the analysis structure students should apply to each: name forces, classify, compare, predict.
Students work individually through the scenarios, producing a structured written analysis for each.
Class discussion of two or three scenarios where student predictions diverged — teacher draws out the reasoning that resolves each disagreement.
Students write a two-sentence summary of what force analysis requires, as if explaining to a student who missed the whole chapter.

periods.teacher_notes: This closing unit asks students to work as force analysts — applying every tool the chapter has built. It builds on all previous units rather than any single one; remind students that their classification work, spring balance readings, and buoyancy explanations are all resources for the scenario analysis. Watch for students who correctly name forces but fail to compare their magnitudes when predicting outcomes — the prediction step is where the highest-order reasoning lives.

coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Students move objects in varied ways and analyse everyday force situations to discover that force is a push or pull arising from interaction and producing one of four observable effects on an object.
coverage_handoff.implied_lo: Students can state the definition of force as a push or pull resulting from interaction between two objects and identify which of the four effects (start motion, change speed, change direction, change shape) a given force produces.

coverage_handoff.stage_label: Classify forces by contact and non-contact
coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Students investigate and classify all five force types — muscular force, friction, magnetic force, electrostatic force, and gravitational force — into contact and non-contact categories by examining the conditions under which each operates.
coverage_handoff.implied_lo: Students can classify any given force example as contact or non-contact, name its type, identify the two interacting objects, and state one distinguishing condition for that force type.

coverage_handoff.stage_label: Measure weight and distinguish mass from weight
coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Students use a spring balance to measure the weight of objects in newtons, identify the instrument's range and least count, and apply the mass-versus-weight distinction by reasoning about how weight varies across planetary locations while mass remains constant.
coverage_handoff.implied_lo: Students can measure the weight of an object using a spring balance (correctly identifying range and least count), record the reading in newtons, and explain why the same object has a different weight on different planets while its mass stays the same.

coverage_handoff.stage_label: Explain floating and sinking through competing forces
coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Students investigate upthrust through direct observation, apply the force-balance framework to explain floating and sinking, and use Archimedes' Principle alongside the density argument to explain why objects of varying density behave differently in liquids — integrating force classification, measurement reasoning, and causal explanation.
coverage_handoff.implied_lo: Students can explain the outcome of any given floating or sinking scenario by naming and comparing the gravitational force and buoyant force acting on the object, applying Archimedes' Principle where relevant, and connecting the explanation to the broader classification of forces as physical causes of change in the world.

assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can state the definition of force as a push or pull resulting from interaction between two objects and identify which of the four effects (start motion, change speed, change direction, change shape) a given force produces.

competency.competency_text: Understanding the physical world through the concept of force as the agent governing changes in motion, direction, and shape.

assessment_items.question_text: A goalkeeper catches a football that is moving towards the goal. Which effect of force best describes what happens to the football?

options.label: A
options.text: The force changes the direction of the football without affecting its speed.

options.label: B
options.text: The force changes the shape of the football permanently.

options.label: C
options.text: The force changes the speed of the moving football.

options.label: D
options.text: The force starts the football moving from rest.

what_each_option_reveals.D: Selecting this option indicates the student has confused the effect of a force on a stationary object with the effect on a moving object — a confusion between two of the four effect categories.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Selecting this option indicates the student associates a hand catching a ball with squashing or deforming it, over-applying the shape-change effect and not recognising that catching primarily decelerates the ball.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Selecting this option indicates the student has partially correct reasoning — catching does involve a direction change in some situations — but misses that the goalkeeper stops the ball, making speed change the primary and more precise effect here.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students who struggle with sport contexts can be prompted to think of any moving object being stopped by a hand. The question accepts either 'slowing to zero' or 'stopping' as valid mental models of speed change.

assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can state the definition of force as a push or pull resulting from interaction between two objects and identify which of the four effects (start motion, change speed, change direction, change shape) a given force produces.

competency.competency_text: Understanding the physical world through the concept of force as the agent governing changes in motion, direction, and shape.

assessment_items.question_text: According to the formal definition established in this chapter, which statement best describes what a force is?

options.label: A
options.text: A force is a push or pull on an object resulting from that object's interaction with another object.

options.label: B
options.text: A force is any form of energy transferred from one object to another.

options.label: C
options.text: A force is the speed at which an object moves after being hit.

options.label: D
options.text: A force is the weight of an object measured in kilograms.

what_each_option_reveals.B: Selecting this option reveals a confusion between force and energy — a common carry-over misconception from everyday language where 'force' and 'energy' are used interchangeably.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Selecting this option indicates the student has conflated force with the resulting motion or speed, not recognising force as the cause rather than the effect.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Selecting this option reveals a confusion between force and mass/weight — likely because kilograms appear in weight discussions; the student has not yet separated the measurement of matter from the definition of force.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students who are more comfortable with Tamil or another home language can be encouraged to translate the definition and check whether the interaction idea is preserved. Pointing to the box-pushing activity from the chapter as a concrete anchor helps students who are not yet confident with formal definitions.

assessment_items.stage_label: Classify forces by contact and non-contact
assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can classify any given force example as contact or non-contact, name its type, identify the two interacting objects, and state one distinguishing condition for that force type.

competency.competency_text: Understanding the physical world through the concept of force as the agent governing changes in motion, direction, and shape.

assessment_items.question_text: A charged plastic scale held near small paper pieces attracts them without touching them. Which force is acting and what is its correct classification?

options.label: A
options.text: Electrostatic force; contact force because the scale must eventually touch the paper to move it

options.label: B
options.text: Electrostatic force; non-contact force

options.label: C
options.text: Magnetic force; non-contact force

options.label: D
options.text: Muscular force; contact force because the student's hand caused the movement

what_each_option_reveals.C: Selecting this option reveals a confusion between magnetic force and electrostatic force — both are non-contact forces in the chapter, so the student has the category right but has not distinguished the conditions (charge vs. magnetism) that produce each.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Selecting this option reveals the misconception that a non-contact force becomes a contact force if the objects eventually touch; the student does not recognise that the classification depends on whether contact is required for the force to act, not on what happens afterward.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Selecting this option shows the student is attributing the cause to the nearest human action (the student's hand) rather than identifying the scientific force acting between the charged scale and the paper.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students who are unsure about 'charged' can be directed back to the rubbing activity with polythene — the question mirrors that exact scenario. Students who classify correctly but give the wrong force name can be credited for partial understanding.

Surface | Stopping distance (relative)
Glass | Short
Ceramic tile | Short
Wood | Medium
Cloth | Long
Sand | Longest
assessment_items.question_text: A student pushes an identical object across five different surfaces and records the stopping distance for each. Refer to the table provided. Which conclusion correctly identifies the force responsible and explains the pattern?

options.label: A
options.text: Friction; surfaces with more irregularities interlock more with the object, producing a greater opposing force and a longer stopping distance.

options.label: B
options.text: Friction; surfaces with more irregularities interlock more with the object, producing a greater opposing force and a shorter stopping distance.

options.label: C
options.text: Gravitational force; heavier surfaces pull the object to a stop more quickly.

options.label: D
options.text: Muscular force; the student applied different amounts of push on each surface, causing the different stopping distances.

what_each_option_reveals.C: Selecting this option reveals a misconception that gravity varies with surface type, confusing gravitational force with the surface-contact force that actually causes stopping.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Selecting this option shows the student correctly identifies the force and mechanism but reverses the relationship between friction and stopping distance — a logical inversion error suggesting the causal direction is not fully understood.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Selecting this option reveals a failure to control variables — the student attributes the difference in stopping distance to a difference in applied force rather than recognising the experimental design kept the push constant.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students who struggle with the table can be asked to simply name the surface that stopped the object fastest and the surface that stopped it slowest before attempting to choose an option. This narrows the reasoning task to the core pattern.

assessment_items.stage_label: Classify forces by contact and non-contact
assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can classify any given force example as contact or non-contact, name its type, identify the two interacting objects, and state one distinguishing condition for that force type.

competency.competency_text: Understanding the physical world through the concept of force as the agent governing changes in motion, direction, and shape.

assessment_items.question_text: Two ring magnets are placed on a vertical stick with their like poles facing each other. The upper magnet appears to float without touching the lower one. Identify the force acting on the upper magnet that prevents it from falling, classify it, name the two interacting objects, and state one condition that distinguishes this force from electrostatic force.
expected_elements: Names the force as magnetic force.
Classifies it correctly as a non-contact force.
Identifies the two interacting objects as the upper magnet and the lower magnet.

States one distinguishing condition — e.g. magnetic force acts between magnets or magnetic materials and does not require charge, whereas electrostatic force requires one or both objects to be electrically charged.

SCR.inclusivity: Students who recall the activity but cannot write a formal condition can be asked to describe in their own words what you need to do to a plastic scale before it attracts paper — this prompts the charge condition that distinguishes electrostatic from magnetic force. Drawings of the two setups are also acceptable as supporting evidence for the classification.

assessment_items.stage_label: Measure weight and distinguish mass from weight
assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can measure the weight of an object using a spring balance (correctly identifying range and least count), record the reading in newtons, and explain why the same object has a different weight on different planets while its mass stays the same.

competency.competency_text: Measuring physical properties of matter using simple instruments in standard units.

assessment_items.visual_stimulus:
Planet | Weight of 1 kg object (N)
Earth | 10
Moon | 1.6
Mars | 3.8
Venus | 9
Jupiter | 25.4
assessment_items.question_text: A spring balance on Earth reads 10 N when a stone is hung from it. Refer to the table provided. If the same stone is taken to Jupiter, which statement correctly predicts the spring balance reading and explains why the reading changes?

options.label: A
options.text: The spring balance reads 1.6 N on Jupiter because Jupiter is further from the Sun, so gravity is weaker there.

options.label: B
options.text: The spring balance reads 10 N on Jupiter because the stone's mass does not change.

options.label: C
options.text: The spring balance reads 25.4 N on Jupiter because Jupiter's stronger gravitational pull increases the weight of the stone, even though its mass stays the same.

options.label: D
options.text: The spring balance reads 25.4 N on Jupiter because the stone gains more matter when moved to a planet with stronger gravity.

what_each_option_reveals.B: Selecting this option reveals the persistent mass-equals-weight misconception — the student correctly knows mass does not change but incorrectly concludes that weight therefore also does not change.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Selecting this option reveals a deeper misconception: that moving to a stronger gravitational field adds matter to the object, confusing the concept of mass (amount of matter) with a property that can be altered by location.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Selecting this option reveals a confusion about which planet has the strongest gravity, combined with a false rule about distance from the Sun — the student is applying an incorrect generalisation rather than reading or reasoning from the data.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students who are uncertain can be directed to the planet table and asked to simply find the Jupiter row before attempting to choose an option. Encouraging students to substitute 'gravitational force on the stone' for 'weight' in their reasoning helps those who confuse the two words.

assessment_items.stage_label: Measure weight and distinguish mass from weight
assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can measure the weight of an object using a spring balance (correctly identifying range and least count), record the reading in newtons, and explain why the same object has a different weight on different planets while its mass stays the same.

competency.competency_text: Measuring physical properties of matter using simple instruments in standard units.

assessment_items.question_text: A spring balance has a maximum reading of 10 N and 50 equally spaced divisions on its scale. What is the least count of this spring balance, and what does the least count tell a student about making measurements with it?

options.label: A
options.text: Least count is 0.2 N; it tells the student the smallest difference in weight the instrument can distinguish.

options.label: B
options.text: Least count is 0.2 N; it tells the student the weight of one division mark on the scale.

options.label: C
options.text: Least count is 10 N; it tells the student the heaviest object that can be weighed.

options.label: D
options.text: Least count is 5 N; it is found by dividing the number of divisions by the maximum reading.

what_each_option_reveals.C: Selecting this option shows the student has confused 'range' (the maximum reading) with 'least count', indicating these two instrument properties have not been distinguished.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Selecting this option shows the student can calculate least count correctly but misinterprets its meaning — confusing 'the value of one division' (a true statement about the scale) with 'the smallest distinguishable difference' (the operationally correct meaning of least count in measurement); this is a subtle but important distinction.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Selecting this option reveals a procedural error: the student has inverted the least-count formula, dividing divisions by range instead of range by divisions.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students who struggle with the calculation can be asked to first state how many divisions fit into the full range, which scaffolds the division step. Allowing students to draw a miniature scale and mark ten divisions can also make the concept of 'one division value' concrete.

assessment_items.stage_label: Measure weight and distinguish mass from weight
assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can measure the weight of an object using a spring balance (correctly identifying range and least count), record the reading in newtons, and explain why the same object has a different weight on different planets while its mass stays the same.

competency.competency_text: Measuring physical properties of matter using simple instruments in standard units.

assessment_items.question_text: Arjun uses a spring balance to measure the weight of his pencil box on Earth and records 2.4 N. He then claims: 'If I take my pencil box to the Moon, the spring balance will still read 2.4 N because the pencil box has not changed.' Identify the error in Arjun's reasoning, state what the spring balance would actually read on the Moon, and explain what has changed and what has not.
expected_elements: Identifies the error: Arjun has confused mass (which does not change) with weight (which does change with location).
States that the spring balance on the Moon would read a value smaller than 2.4 N (approximately 0.38 N, or correctly derived as 2.4 × 1.6/10), because the Moon's gravitational pull is weaker.

Explains that mass (the amount of matter in the pencil box) stays the same, but weight (the gravitational force Earth or the Moon exerts on it) changes because the Moon's gravity is weaker than Earth's.

SCR.inclusivity: Students who are uncertain about the Moon value can be given credit for correctly identifying the conceptual error (mass vs. weight confusion) and stating directionally that the reading would decrease, even if they do not calculate the exact value. Students who prefer to draw a diagram showing a spring balance with a smaller stretch on the Moon can do so as supporting evidence.

assessment_items.stage_label: Explain floating and sinking through competing forces
assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can explain the outcome of any given floating or sinking scenario by naming and comparing the gravitational force and buoyant force acting on the object, applying Archimedes' Principle where relevant, and connecting the explanation to the broader classification of forces as physical causes of change in the world.

competency.competency_text: Understanding the physical world through the concept of force as the agent governing changes in motion, direction, and shape.

assessment_items.question_text: A sealed empty bottle is pushed to the bottom of a bucket of water and then released. Which explanation correctly identifies the forces acting and predicts what will happen?

options.label: A
options.text: Buoyant force acts upward and gravitational force acts downward; since buoyant force is greater than gravitational force for the bottle, it rises to the surface.

options.label: B
options.text: Buoyant force acts upward and gravitational force acts downward; since they are equal for any object in water, the bottle stays wherever it is placed.

options.label: C
options.text: Only gravitational force acts on the bottle; it pulls the bottle down and the bottle stays at the bottom.

options.label: D
options.text: The bottle rises because it is light, and light objects always float — no force comparison is needed.

what_each_option_reveals.C: Selecting this option reveals the misconception that gravity is the only force acting on submerged objects — the student has not incorporated buoyant force into their model.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Selecting this option reveals a partial understanding: the student knows both forces exist but incorrectly generalises that they are always equal, not recognising that equilibrium depends on the object's specific properties.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Selecting this option reveals that the student is using an intuitive size-or-weight rule ('light things float') rather than the force-comparison framework — they are bypassing the causal mechanism entirely.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students who are uncertain can be asked to describe what they felt when they pushed a bottle into water in the chapter activity before choosing an option. Students who choose correctly but cannot explain why can be asked to draw a force diagram to scaffold their verbal explanation.

assessment_items.stage_label: Explain floating and sinking through competing forces
assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can explain the outcome of any given floating or sinking scenario by naming and comparing the gravitational force and buoyant force acting on the object, applying Archimedes' Principle where relevant, and connecting the explanation to the broader classification of forces as physical causes of change in the world.

competency.competency_text: Understanding the physical world through the concept of force as the agent governing changes in motion, direction, and shape.

assessment_items.question_text: Pumice is a volcanic rock full of air pockets. Despite being a rock, it floats on water. Using Archimedes' Principle, which explanation correctly accounts for this?

options.label: A
options.text: Pumice floats because it has a very large surface area in contact with water, which increases the upward force beyond what gravity exerts.

options.label: B
options.text: Pumice floats because rocks are always less dense than water.

options.label: C
options.text: Pumice floats because the air pockets create an upward thrust inside the rock that directly pushes it above the water surface.

options.label: D
options.text: Pumice floats because the weight of water it displaces is greater than the weight of the pumice itself, so the upward buoyant force exceeds gravitational force.

what_each_option_reveals.B: Selecting this option reveals a sweeping generalisation error — the student has inverted the density rule ('rocks sink') without precision, not connecting the floating to density being less than water specifically because of air pockets.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Selecting this option reveals a mechanistic misconception: the student imagines the air as actively pushing the rock up from within rather than understanding that air pockets reduce the overall density of the pumice so that the displaced water weighs more than the pumice.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Selecting this option reveals a confusion between surface area and buoyant force — the student incorrectly introduces surface area as a determinant of upthrust, which is not how Archimedes' Principle works.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students who are uncertain about Archimedes' Principle can be asked to first state what the principle says about the upward force (equals weight of displaced liquid) before evaluating the options. Students who struggle with 'density' can think of pumice as a mostly-air object that happens to have some rock in it.

assessment_items.stage_label: Explain floating and sinking through competing forces
assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can explain the outcome of any given floating or sinking scenario by naming and comparing the gravitational force and buoyant force acting on the object, applying Archimedes' Principle where relevant, and connecting the explanation to the broader classification of forces as physical causes of change in the world.

competency.competency_text: Understanding the physical world through the concept of force as the agent governing changes in motion, direction, and shape.

assessment_items.question_text: A large steel ship floats on the ocean, yet a small solid steel ball sinks. Both are made of the same material. Explain this apparent contradiction using the concepts of gravitational force, buoyant force, and Archimedes' Principle. In your explanation, state what the ship is designed to do differently from the solid ball that allows it to float, and identify what type of force buoyant force is.
look_for: Correctly identifies that gravitational force pulls both the ship and ball downward, and buoyant force acts upward on both.
Applies Archimedes' Principle: the upward force equals the weight of displaced water, so an object floats when the weight of water it displaces equals or exceeds its own weight.

Explains that the ship displaces a large volume of water because of its hollow, bowl-like shape — meaning the weight of displaced water can equal the ship's total weight, so buoyant force balances gravitational force.

Explains that the solid steel ball displaces only a small volume of water relative to its weight, so the displaced water weighs less than the ball — buoyant force is smaller than gravitational force, and the ball sinks.
Identifies buoyant force as a contact force (the water and the ship/ball are the two interacting objects).

ECR.inclusivity: Students who find the ship scenario abstract can be directed to the sealed bottle activity: the air inside the bottle made it displace more water than its own weight. The ship works on the same principle — it is essentially a giant sealed container. Students who cannot write the full explanation can be asked to draw a force diagram for each object and annotate it, which can carry partial credit.

assessment_items.task: Refer to the table provided. For each of the four scenarios: (1) name both forces acting on the object and state their directions, (2) classify each force as contact or non-contact, (3) state which force is greater (or whether they balance), and (4) write one sentence explaining the predicted outcome in terms of the force comparison.
assessment_items.scaffold: For each row: start by identifying what is causing each force (which two objects are interacting). Then decide whether those objects are touching. Use that to classify contact or non-contact. Finally, compare the two forces to explain why the object behaves as it does.
format_of_output: Completed table with all columns filled for all four scenarios.
One written sentence per scenario explaining the predicted outcome in force-comparison terms.

OPEN_TASK.format_type: Classification or sorting task with justification
OPEN_TASK.format_rationale: The final stage's implied LO requires students to integrate force classification, gravitational reasoning, and buoyancy into a single analytical act — the classification-with-justification format is the most natural vehicle because it asks students to name, sort, and causally explain simultaneously, demonstrating the convergent operation of both co-central competencies.
OPEN_TASK.what_this_demonstrates: A complete response demonstrates that the student can identify the specific forces at work in any physical scenario, apply the contact/non-contact classification accurately, compare force magnitudes to determine outcomes, and connect those explanations to both the force-classification framework and the buoyancy/gravitational framework developed across the chapter.
OPEN_TASK.reading_the_scaffold: The scaffold guides students to decompose the analysis into two prior steps (identify interacting objects, determine contact) before reaching the comparison step. A teacher reading responses should check whether students who fill columns 4–7 correctly also write sentences in column 9 that are genuinely causal rather than simply restating the column entries.
OPEN_TASK.strong_vs_weak_markers: Strong responses name both forces with correct directions for all four rows, correctly classify each as contact or non-contact, and write sentences that explicitly compare the two forces to explain the outcome. Weak responses either leave the direction or classification blank, or write outcome sentences that describe what happens without referencing forces ('the block floats because wood floats in water').
OPEN_TASK.inclusivity: Students who find the table format difficult can be permitted to write their four analyses as paragraphs using the scaffold questions as paragraph prompts. Students who are uncertain about the magnet scenario can be directed back to the floating ring-magnet activity and asked what force prevented the upper magnet from falling onto the lower one.
